scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4630: One of our IT lab machines (the one called it_lab3)
has dropped off the network completely -- from that machine you cannot reach
anything at all, not even the first thing it is supposed to talk to. The
other machines around it are all fine; it is just that one. The student who
uses it did not change anything, so stop looking at our end. Someone here
has already called it: its port died. I couldn't tell you what a port is,
but it is your equipment, and one machine does not cut itself off. Find out
why that one machine is cut off and put it back on today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. it_lab3 has its IP on 192.168.1.0/24, reaches its
  gateway (192.168.1.1) with 0% loss, and RIP is converged so it reaches other
  segments too. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a single-host isolation that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- it_lab3 is totally isolated
and cannot reach even its gateway -- is NOT reproducible: it_lab3 holds its
192.168.1.0/24 address, reaches its default gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss, and
(RIP being converged on router0/router1/router2) reaches off-segment destinations as
well.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: it_lab3 is fully connected and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the it_lab3 -> gateway path
(and an off-segment ping), finds it working, checks the host's interface/route, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a dead port or isolated host to satisfy the
ticket is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported fault does not exist. A thorough end-to-end inspection of every component in `it_lab3`'s data path found nothing wrong.

`it_lab3`'s network interface eth0 is physically and logically UP (LOWER_UP flag set), correctly addressed as 192.168.1.5/24 with a default gateway of 192.168.1.1 (router0), and has zero TX/RX errors or drops. No iptables rules are in place on the host. Switch0, which bridges the `lan_it` segment to router0, has both ports in the bridge and is forwarding correctly. Router0's RIP configuration properly announces all three of its connected networks (192.168.1.0/24, 192.168.2.0/24, 10.0.0.0/8), and all three routers have complete, consistent RIP routing tables covering every subnet in the topology.

Live ping tests confirm full bidirectional reachability: `it_lab3` can reach its on-subnet peers (it_hod, it_lab1–it_lab4), the first-hop gateway, router interfaces across two WAN hops, the servers LAN host pc1 (1.0.0.5), and the internet LAN host pc2 (128.168.0.2)—all at 0% packet loss. Reciprocal pings from pc1 and pc2 back to 192.168.1.5 succeed equally.

The helpdesk ticket's claim that `it_lab3`'s port has died and that the machine cannot reach anything is factually incorrect. The network is healthy. No corrective action is needed; the caller should re-verify at the physical workstation, as the fault, if any, is at the application or user level, not in the network infrastructure.
